Question 1 · put them in execution order

Five script tags.
One order.

<!-- every one of these is discovered by the parser at the same moment -->
A  <script async src="a.js"></script>         // downloads in 300ms
B  <script defer src="b.js"></script>         // downloads in 200ms
C  <script defer src="c.js"></script>         // downloads in 300ms
D  <script async src="d.js"></script>         // downloads in  50ms
E  <script async defer src="e.js"></script>   // downloads in  60ms
Assume the HTML takes 320 ms to parse and every download starts the moment the tag is seen.
MODULE 01 · VIDEO 5
03 / 35
Question 1 · the answer

D, E, A, B, C.

The Rules

• async executes immediately upon download (unpredictable order).
• defer waits for the HTML parser, preserving document order.

The Trap: Script E

Both keywords present? async wins.
E downloads in 80ms, so it executes right after D.

Question 7 · match them up

Six vitals.
Six descriptions.

  • TTFB1 · The time it takes for a webpage to respond to a user's first interaction.
  • FID2 · The time that the main thread is blocked from responding to user input.
  • TTI3 · The average time it takes for a webpage to update its visuals after a user interacts with it.
  • TBT4 · The time it takes for the server to respond to a request and start sending data back to the client.
  • CLS5 · The time it takes for a webpage to be fully loaded and responsive to user input.
  • INP6 · The stability of a webpage's layout — the unexpected layout shifts that occur as it loads.
MODULE 01 · VIDEO 6
17 / 35
Question 7 · the answer

Four are clocks. One is a sum.
One is not time at all.

Clocks (ms)

• TTFB: time to first byte
• FCP: first pixel painted
• LCP: main content visible
• INP: click to painted frame

Sum (ms)

• TBT: sum of all blocking tasks exceeding 50ms between FCP and TTI.

Score (unitless)

• CLS: visual stability score.
Distance fraction × Impact fraction.

MODULE 01 · VIDEO 6
18 / 35
Q7 · why — TTFB, and everything that happens before it

The first byte,
not the last one.

DNS, TCP and TLS all finish before the request is even sent — and all three are on the clock. TTFB stops at the moment the first byte of the response arrives, because that is the moment the parser can start work. The rest of the response is still on the wire behind it.
MODULE 01 · VIDEO 6
19 / 35
Q7 · why — FID, and the 50ms line

The click that arrives
while the thread is busy.

FID measures the wait, not the handler. And it is a fragile number: click a moment earlier and it is near zero, click a moment later and it is 300ms — same page, same code. If the user never interacts, there is no value at all. That fragility is exactly why INP replaced it.
MODULE 01 · VIDEO 6
20 / 35
Q7 · why — the number TTI hides

Same TTI.
700ms versus 15ms.

Both pages become reliably interactive at the same instant, so TTI scores them identically. On page A the user could do nothing at all for three quarters of a second; on page B they could act between every slice. TBT is the metric that tells the two apart — it measures how interactive the page was on the way to being interactive.
MODULE 01 · VIDEO 6
21 / 35
Q7 · why — CLS, the one with no clock

Distance × impact.
No unit, no milliseconds.

Same bug, two scores. The banner moved everything, so its impact fraction is 1 and the distance goes straight through. The filter bar left the header alone, so 40% of the screen never moved and the score drops by two thirds. Reserve the box before the content arrives — width and height on images, min-height on slots, aspect-ratio on embeds — and both scores go to zero.

Question 8 · match them up

Five directives,
five definitions.

  • no-cache1 · Validates a stale response with the origin server before using it.
  • must-revalidate2 · Serves stale content while validating the cached response with the origin server.
  • no-store3 · Does not cache any part of the request or the response.
  • private4 · Validates the cached resource with the origin before using it, even if it is still fresh.
  • stale-while-revalidate5 · Prevents caching on shared caches.

23 / 35
Question 8 · the answer: no-cache

no-cache = always revalidate.
Two round trips, one nearly free.

An ETag is a hash of the file. The browser sends the one it holds; the server compares and either says nothing changed in a few hundred bytes, or sends the new file.

Question 11 · what gets logged on click

Seven listeners.
One click.

<div id="outer"> <div id="middle"> <button id="btn">Click</button> </div> </div>

outer .addEventListener('click', () => log('A'), true)
outer .addEventListener('click', () => log('B'))
middle.addEventListener('click', () => log('C'), true)
middle.addEventListener('click', (e) => { log('D'); e.stopPropagation() })
middle.addEventListener('click', () => log('E'))
btn   .addEventListener('click', () => log('G'), true)
btn   .addEventListener('click', () => log('F'))
The third argument is capture. Where it is missing, the listener runs on the way back up.

Q12 · the trap

Only one of these
brackets is free.

:where(…)

Always 0.
Adds zero specificity, perfect for library defaults.

:not(…)

Not free.
Takes the specificity of its highest argument.

:has(…)

Not free.
Same rule — most specific argument counts.

/* the library ships this */
:where(.button) { padding: 8px 16px }   0-0-0
It offers a default — it never insists.
/* you ship this */
.my-button { margin: 20px }          0-1-0 → wins
One plain class overrides it. No !important.
Wrap resets and defaults in :where() so consumers can easily override them without fighting !important.
